Du Hood à la scène: From the Hood to the Stage
Samira : Tu ne parlais pas des choses do: Samira: Were you not talking about the things you wanted to talk about?
Bien connu des jeunes Montréalais, Anas: Well known among young Montrealers, Anas Hassouna is killing it on social media with his colleague Oussama Fares. The young comedian produces a huge amount of content across a variety of media through his company, Fishnet. It ranges from comedy videos on TikTok to their YouTube show On est là. On it, they talk with various public figures, from Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois to Fabrice Vil.
L’École Converse a rencontré Anas Hassou: École Converse met with Anas Hassouna to understand the man who brings the codes of his neighbourhood, the Hood, to the stage.
<strong>Naila : Anas, peux-tu nous parle: Naila: Anas, can you tell us about your journey?
Mon parcours est quand même atypique. Mo: My path is pretty atypical. Me and my patnais, Oussama Fares, we've known each other for over 15 years, from Montréal-Nord. Since we were little kids, we've known we wanted to crack jokes. After that, I moved to Repentigny during high school. I was already doing improv, but there, I discovered real improv. After that, my guidance counsellor called my parents to tell them I wasn't going to go into accounting. I had told them I was going to the École de l'humour.
Donc, à l’École de l’humour, j’ai rencon: So, at the École de l'humour, I met Romane. And, with my boy Lamine and Oussama, we started a collective. Oussama and Lamine bought equipment, and we slowly started making videos. We ended up making videos in front of the camera and also behind the camera for a lot of comedians. It was kind of new, starting to make short clips. Then, little by little, we started working for Just for Laughs. A few years later, I started working a lot more on stage. Oussama Fares got into stage work recently, and so on, and here we are today.
J’étais moins à l’avant de la scène. Auj: I was less front and centre on stage. Today, I have a pretty good career, hamdoulilah. My path has still been complicated, because not all institutions are equipped to receive the baggage we can bring as immigrants and all that. So, that's a very big summary of my journey.
<strong>Ahmed : Ce que je remarque, c’es: Ahmed: What I notice is that you took a different path from many other comedians from minority backgrounds. What do you say to that?
Oussama et moi, on a emprunté une voie q: Oussama and I took a path that nobody else wanted to take, and that nobody else could actually take. We represent the street. We represent that in part because we come from there and all. Our path is special because it isn't mainstream. It's dangerous because we represent people who are still a minority, and we're trying to open things up. We want to represent all of Quebec, to be a bridge with that stuff, but it takes balls, you know. I made choices, though. It's clear who I represent. So if that audience decides I don't represent them anymore, it's over, because we showed our colours.
<strong>Marc-Elder : Comment s’est dérou: Marc-Elder: How was your time at the École de l'humour?
Le personnel était accueillant et tout,: The staff were welcoming and all, but at that point it wasn't possible for me to draw on the very Montréal references I have, to be 100% myself. I was mostly a… polished, atrophied version, I'd say. An amputated version, because I only did what the mainstream Quebec audience could understand.
<strong>Samira : Tu ne parlais pas des c: Samira: Were you not talking about the things you wanted to talk about?
Je n’avais personne à qui en parler, en: I had nobody to talk to about it, actually. It's not that I was being stopped or anything. It's just that I was with 12 other white people, and we performed in front of a white audience, and we had white teachers. I just didn't feel I had the space to do what I do today at that point, but I was also still developing and all. That's why I want to be clear that I'm not saying anything bad about the School. Nobody ever pushed me to do something I'm not. I had a lot of latitude, actually.
Moi, dans ma tête, je me disais, si j’ar: Me, in my head, I was thinking, if I show up and say, “Yo, what's up? Feeling good, ranceuse?” I'd have 12 people staring at me wide-eyed. I didn't have the space because it was a bit less suited to that. It's good, because I got the chance to do something that hadn't been done yet. It's true that you have to be careful with comedy. When you do comedy in front of white people, and you talk about your ethnic side, it's insidious. You can end up doing a disservice to the people you represent. You have to be careful before casting stones at the artist.
Ce qui nous inspire, c’est la vie de tou: What inspires us is everyday life, it's where we come from, man. It's an immigrant mother helping her family survive. It's our parents. It's our journeys. It's the journeys of the people around us. It's really atypical stuff.
Tu viens du <em>Hood</em>, tu vois des c: You come from the Hood, you see things you wouldn't see elsewhere, especially as the son of immigrants. For me, what inspires me is my parents, honestly. The further I go, the more that's true. My parents, it's the classic story. Two people who worked really hard, and they raise you in that, and they explain racism to you, and how you live it. My dad always told me: “You have to be twice or three times as good as the others, otherwise they'll take them anyway.”
<strong>Marc-Elder : Comment tes parents: Marc-Elder: How did your parents take your career choice?
Mes parents, que Dieu me les garde, étai: My parents, God keep them for me, were very angry that I went into comedy. Like good parents. If you have parents who encourage you right from the start when you tell them you're going into comedy, I think you don't have very good parents. Or else they're rich. But my parents didn't agree, and that's normal. They immigrated here. They suffered terribly to come here, and it's really harder than people think, immigrating here. And then you tell them you want to be a comedian – that's pretty rough. They must have suspected it. I've always done improv. I've always had problems because I talk too much. But they had expectations, because I had good grades. I kind of broke their expectations, but today, they're happy. They're starting to look forward to my big break. My mother came to the last Olympia show I did.
Aujourd’hui, mes parents sont mes plus g: Today, my parents are my biggest supporters.
C’est large. J’ai écouté beaucoup d’humo: It's broad. I listened to a lot of Quebec comedy. Before Rachid Badouri, there was Laurent Paquin, Mario Jean for Quebec comedy, and internationally, there was Jamal, Dieudonné back when it was halal to listen to him. I was a geek. I listened to everything. But when Rachid Badouri arrived, it changed everything [...] Quebec wasn't ready for Rachid's level. It took a Rachid, a friendly Arab, who dances and all… and who's very funny on light topics. He couldn't have been an Arab Guillaume Wagner, say, right from the start. It never would have worked.
‍<strong>Fatima : Vous vous sentez barré: ‍Fatima: Do you sometimes feel shut out?
Ça existe, mais c’est aussi parce qu’on: It exists, but it's also because we're independent, and we refused to take the paths of the big machine. We've been approached about that several times. There's the independence, and the fact that racism in Quebec is 100% present, and if you're Black or Arab, they'll throw obstacles in your way. Not necessarily stop you, but throw obstacles in your way. There's a glass ceiling. It's actually concrete, the ceiling.
<strong>Samira : Certains humoristes com: Samira: Some comedians like Arnaud Soly or Virginie Despentes fully embrace politically engaged comedy. Would you say it's harder for you to adopt that type of comedy?
Il faut que je fasse attention, dépendam: I have to be careful, depending on what we're talking about, because, say, if I say something that the old-stock Quebec community doesn't like, I'm a radical, extremist leftist. And if I say something that my own community doesn't like, I'm a sellout. So, yeah. 100%. I'm always caught between a rock and a hard place. Absolutely.
<strong>Marc-Elder : Dans le fond, est-c: Marc-Elder: Deep down, do you think you wouldn't have the right to go as far as Mike Ward?
Moi, c’est clair. Déjà, Mike Ward, on tr: For me, it's clear. Already, with Mike Ward, people think he doesn't have the right to go as far as Mike Ward! If you're Arab, it's worse. If you come from elsewhere, it's 100% worse. I don't remember which study came out on how, say, police officers or people in positions of power always tend to be more lenient with white people than with Black people for the same thing. That's 100% true for me too.
<strong>Samira : Est-ce que tu penses qu: Samira: Do you think it's possible to break into comedy when you don't come from a well-off background?
Non, je trouve que nous [Anas et Oussama: No, I think we [Anas and Oussama] are proof that no. My parents helped me pay for the École de l'humour. They had an income that gave me access to loans and bursaries. But comedy is the people's art. From the moment you can talk to people on Instagram, on your phone, and you have a pen and a sheet of paper on which you can write jokes and try them out. Being well-off helps with everything, but it isn't necessary in comedy.
<strong>Marc-Elder : Penses-tu qu’on peu: Marc-Elder: Do you think you can joke about anything?
Je pense que, la limite, c’est si les ge: I think the limit is whether the people concerned are laughing. That's really the only limit I make a point of respecting.
<strong>Fatima : Pourquoi ton entreprise: Fatima: Why is your company called Fishnet?
Il y a un rappeur originaire de Montréal: There's a rapper from Montréal-Nord named Telus. He often said: “Fish cale, rich cale. Toutes mes finzs dansent.” Fish cale represents drugs, and the finzs represent the consumers, the addicts. And we see ourselves as if we were selling drugs. We're joke dealers. That's why we drew that parallel. Our path is really rap-inspired. It's always been about being a crew. And the name “Fishnet” comes from the words “Fiscale”.
<strong>Naila : Est-ce que vous recevez: Naila: Do you get a lot of comments from people telling you that you represent them in what you do?
Oui et on est là, c’est comme ramener le: Yes, and with On est là, it's like bringing the Hood into a big, well-produced show, with interviews and people who don't necessarily come from the Hood. With the show, On est là, we got a lot of comments saying, “You represent us.” And it's good to be represented outside of religion and for the wrong reasons. It's the one that makes us happiest, after “You're funny.”
<strong>Ahmed : Pour les jeunes de Montr: Ahmed: For the young people in Montréal-Nord and Saint-Michel who follow you, what do you think your journey can pass on to them?
Ça peut leur léguer l’impression qu’ils: It can give them the sense that they can make it too, because we started from nothing. And above all, it can make them want to do it. And the one piece of advice I want to give to anyone, no matter the field, is: do it as early as possible; just do it, even if you're bad, do it; and if it's what you want to do, do it. There's nothing better than experience. It might not work right away, it might not work in six or seven years, because you have to love it enough to face that reality, but do it. Because if it works, you'll realize that those years when there were no results were actually really important, because nothing replaces experience.
